A display apparatus includes counter electrodes that function both as common electrodes during image display and as scan electrodes during touch detection. The apparatus also has a first scan circuit for sequentially driving gate lines and a second scan circuit for sequentially driving the counter electrodes.  

In this display apparatus, each frame interval contains a write interval in which one full screen is scanned continuously, and a touch-detection interval positioned between that write interval and the write interval of the following frame.  

The second scan circuit is provided with a shift register section and a switch section. The switch section has a seventh thin-film transistor that supplies a DC driving signal to an output node, and an eighth thin-film transistor that supplies an AC driving signal to the same output node. During the write interval, a second control signal is applied to hold fixed the voltage of a third retention node connected to the gate electrode of the seventh thin-film transistor.
outputs.L3:
The display device is configured so that the counter electrodes serve a dual function. During normal image display, the counter electrodes operate as common electrodes that provide a reference potential for displaying an image. During touch detection, the same counter electrodes are used as scan electrodes for touch sensing. By sharing the electrodes in this way, the device can reduce the number of separate electrode structures, thereby simplifying the panel configuration and helping to reduce thickness and manufacturing complexity.

One frame period of the display device includes at least two main intervals: a write period and a touch sensing period. During the write period, the device continuously scans one screen to write display data to the pixels. After the write period is completed, and before the write period of the next frame begins, the device enters the touch sensing period. In this touch sensing period, the counter electrodes are driven as touch scan electrodes so that the device can detect the presence or position of a touch input.

The device includes a first scan circuit and a second scan circuit. The first scan circuit is used for display operation and scans gate lines connected to the pixels. By sequentially selecting the gate lines, the first scan circuit enables image data to be written into the pixel circuits across the display screen. The second scan circuit is used for touch sensing and scans the counter electrodes. Since the counter electrodes also function as touch scan electrodes, the second scan circuit selectively drives these electrodes during the touch sensing period.

The second scan circuit includes a shift register unit and a switch unit. The shift register unit generates timing signals for sequentially selecting the counter electrodes to be scanned. The switch unit receives these timing signals and controls the output of drive signals to the counter electrodes. In this manner, the second scan circuit can scan the counter electrodes in a predetermined order for touch detection.

The switch unit is formed using thin-film transistors. These thin-film transistors selectively output DC drive signals and AC drive signals to the counter electrodes depending on the operating period of the display device. During the display write period, a DC drive signal may be supplied so that the counter electrodes function as stable common electrodes for image display. During the touch sensing period, an AC drive signal may be supplied so that the counter electrodes operate as scan electrodes for detecting touch.

In addition, the switch unit is controlled by a control signal that fixes the voltage of a retention node during the write period. By fixing the voltage of the retention node while display data is being written, the circuit can maintain stable operation and prevent unintended variations in the drive signals supplied to the counter electrodes. This improves the reliability of both the display operation and the touch sensing operation within the shared-electrode structure.
outputs.L4:
A display device is configured to perform both image display and touch sensing by sharing part of the display structure for the touch detection function. In particular, the device includes pixel electrodes used for image formation and counter electrodes that face the pixel electrodes. These counter electrodes function as common electrodes during a display period, supplying a common potential for image display, and also function as touch scan electrodes during a touch sensing period. By allowing the same electrodes to serve both purposes, the device can reduce the number of dedicated touch electrodes, simplify the panel structure, and support a thinner integrated touch display.

The display device includes a plurality of gate lines, a plurality of signal lines, pixels arranged near intersections of the gate lines and signal lines, and a plurality of counter electrodes arranged over or under the pixel region. A first scan circuit is provided for sequentially driving the gate lines during a write period in which image data is written to the pixels. A second scan circuit is provided for driving the counter electrodes. The operation of these scan circuits is divided between a display write period and a touch sensing period. During the write period, the first scan circuit selects the gate lines so that pixel signals can be written to the corresponding pixels, while the counter electrodes are driven as common electrodes. During the touch sensing period, the second scan circuit scans the counter electrodes as touch detection electrodes so that a change in capacitance caused by a finger or other conductive object can be detected.

The second scan circuit includes a shift register and a switch unit. The shift register generates sequential scan signals corresponding to the counter electrodes, thereby selecting which counter electrode or group of counter electrodes is to be driven at a given timing. The switch unit receives signals from the shift register and selectively outputs drive signals to the counter electrodes. The switch unit includes transistors that enable different types of drive output, including a DC drive output and an AC drive output. The DC drive output may be used when the counter electrodes operate as common electrodes for display, while the AC drive output may be used when the counter electrodes operate as touch scan electrodes during touch detection. In this way, the second scan circuit can selectively supply appropriate voltages or waveforms to the counter electrodes according to the operating period of the display device.

A retention node is provided in the second scan circuit or in association with the switch unit. This retention node holds a voltage or control state used to determine the output condition of the switch unit. During the writing of display data, the potential of the retention node may be susceptible to fluctuation due to coupling noise, switching noise, or changes in nearby signal lines. If the retention node becomes unstable, the counter electrodes may not be driven correctly, which could degrade display quality or reduce the accuracy of touch sensing.

To address this issue, a control signal is applied to stabilize the retention node during the write period. The control signal maintains the retention node at a desired potential or prevents unintended voltage variation while the gate lines are being scanned and image data is being written into the pixels. By stabilizing the retention node, the second scan circuit can reliably control the switch unit and accurately output the intended DC or AC drive signal to the counter electrodes. This improves the stability of the common electrode potential during display operation and enhances the reliability of touch scanning during touch sensing operation.

As a result, the display device can efficiently combine image display and touch detection in a single panel structure. The counter electrodes are shared between the display function and the touch sensing function, while the first and second scan circuits coordinate the timing of gate line scanning and counter electrode driving. The shift register and transistor-based switch unit in the second scan circuit enable flexible electrode driving, and the stabilization of the retention node by the control signal contributes to dependable operation. This configuration improves display quality, reduces circuit malfunction, and supports accurate touch detection in an integrated touch display device.

**The Power of “The”**

The word **“the”** may seem small, but it is one of the most important words in the English language. It is called a definite article, and it helps us talk about something specific. For example, when we say “the book,” we are not talking about any book—we mean a particular book that the speaker and listener both understand.

“The” gives clarity and direction to a sentence. It can point to a person, place, object, or idea that has already been mentioned or is widely known. In phrases like “the sun,” “the Earth,” or “the internet,” the word helps identify something unique or familiar.

Although it is only three letters long, “the” appears constantly in English writing and speech. It connects ideas, makes communication more precise, and helps sentences sound natural. Without “the,” English would feel incomplete and less clear.

In short, **“the” is a tiny word with a big role**. It shows that even the simplest words can be essential to meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise patent-style abstract describing a display device whose counter electrodes serve as both common display electrodes and touch scan electrodes, with separate scan circuits and TFT switch control during write and touch sensing periods.
counterfactuals.output: A display device includes a display panel having pixel electrodes, counter electrodes opposed to the pixel electrodes, and thin film transistor switches coupled to the pixel electrodes. The counter electrodes are commonly used as common electrodes for image display and as touch scan electrodes for touch detection. A display scan circuit supplies display scan signals during a display write period to control the thin film transistor switches and write image signals to the pixel electrodes, while a touch scan circuit supplies touch scan signals to the counter electrodes during a touch sensing period different from the display write period. Switch control circuitry controls the thin film transistor switches to a predetermined state during the touch sensing period to reduce interference between display operation and touch detection, thereby enabling integrated display and touch sensing with a reduced electrode structure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the invention in one paragraph based on a display apparatus having gate-line scanning, counter-electrode scanning, a frame divided into a write period and a touch sensing period, and a second scan circuit with shift register and switch units outputting DC/AC drive signals.
counterfactuals.output: The invention relates to a display apparatus that combines image display and touch sensing by dividing each frame into a write period and a touch sensing period. During the write period, a gate-line scan circuit sequentially scans gate lines to write image data to pixels, while during the touch sensing period a counter-electrode scan circuit scans counter electrodes used for touch detection. The apparatus includes a second scan circuit having shift-register units and switch units that generate and output appropriate drive signals to the counter electrodes. These drive signals may include DC signals for display operation and AC signals for touch sensing, enabling the same counter electrodes to function both as display electrodes and touch-sensing electrodes. This configuration allows coordinated gate-line scanning and counter-electrode scanning, reducing circuit complexity and supporting efficient integration of touch sensing into the display panel.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical description for a touch-integrated display device in which counter electrodes are used for display and touch sensing, including details about seventh and eighth thin-film transistors and a control signal fixing a retention node during the write period.
counterfactuals.output:
A touch-integrated display device may include a display panel having a plurality of pixels arranged in a matrix and a plurality of counter electrodes disposed so as to overlap the pixels. Each counter electrode may be used commonly as a display electrode during a display driving period and as a touch sensing electrode during a touch sensing period. In the display driving period, the counter electrodes may be supplied with a common voltage for image display, and in the touch sensing period, at least some of the counter electrodes may be supplied with a touch driving signal or may be connected to a touch sensing circuit for detecting a change in capacitance caused by a touch input.

Each pixel may include a display element, such as a liquid crystal element or an organic light-emitting element, and a pixel circuit configured to write and retain a data voltage corresponding to an image signal. The pixel circuit may include a plurality of thin-film transistors and at least one storage capacitor. A retention node may be provided in the pixel circuit for holding a voltage corresponding to the written data voltage or a compensated control voltage. The retention node may be electrically connected to a gate electrode or control terminal of a driving transistor, or to one electrode of a storage capacitor, depending on the pixel circuit configuration.

In one embodiment, the pixel circuit includes a seventh thin-film transistor and an eighth thin-film transistor configured to control the electrical state of the retention node. The seventh thin-film transistor may be connected between the retention node and a reference voltage line, initialization voltage line, or another predetermined potential line. The eighth thin-film transistor may be connected between the retention node and a signal line, compensation node, or another internal node of the pixel circuit. The seventh and eighth thin-film transistors may be controlled by respective scan signals, compensation signals, or initialization signals so that the retention node is selectively initialized, coupled, isolated, or refreshed during different operating periods of the pixel.

During a write period in which a data voltage is written into the pixel circuit, a control signal may be applied to at least one of the seventh thin-film transistor and the eighth thin-film transistor so as to fix the voltage of the retention node at a predetermined potential. By fixing the retention node during the write period, unintended fluctuation of the retained voltage caused by capacitive coupling from a data line, scan line, touch electrode, counter electrode, or adjacent signal line can be suppressed. The control signal may maintain the seventh thin-film transistor in an on-state to clamp the retention node to a fixed voltage, or may maintain the eighth thin-film transistor in an on-state to connect the retention node to a stable reference node. Alternatively, the control signal may place one of the seventh and eighth thin-film transistors in an on-state and the other in an off-state to define a stable electrical path for fixing the retention node while preventing leakage or interference from other nodes.

After completion of the write period, the control signal may be changed so that the retention node is electrically floated or isolated from the fixed potential. The written voltage or compensated voltage may then be retained by the storage capacitor during a retention period. Because the retention node is fixed during the write period and isolated thereafter, the pixel circuit can accurately store the desired voltage while reducing noise induced by touch sensing operation, display common-voltage modulation, or parasitic capacitance associated with the counter electrodes.

The counter electrodes may be divided into a plurality of electrode blocks. During display operation, the electrode blocks may receive a common display voltage. During touch sensing operation, the electrode blocks may be sequentially or simultaneously driven with a touch driving waveform, and a sensing circuit may detect capacitance variations of the electrode blocks. Since the counter electrodes are shared between display driving and touch sensing, the device can reduce the number of dedicated touch electrodes and simplify the panel structure. In addition, by fixing the retention node of each pixel circuit during the write period using the control signal applied to the seventh and eighth thin-film transistors, degradation of display quality caused by touch driving noise, common-electrode coupling, or leakage current can be reduced.

Accordingly, the touch-integrated display device can provide both image display and touch detection using shared counter electrodes, while maintaining stable pixel voltage retention. The seventh and eighth thin-film transistors and the control signal for fixing the retention node during the write period contribute to improved write accuracy, reduced flicker, suppressed crosstalk, and enhanced touch/display integration reliability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract for a patent claim about a display device comprising counter electrodes, first and second scan circuits, frame timing with write and touch sensing periods, and a switch unit that selectively outputs DC and AC drive signals through TFTs.
counterfactuals.output: A display device includes a display panel having a plurality of pixel electrodes and a plurality of counter electrodes, a first scan circuit configured to scan signal lines during a display write period, and a second scan circuit configured to scan the counter electrodes during a touch sensing period within a frame period. The frame period includes at least one write period for writing image signals to pixels and at least one touch sensing period for detecting a touch input using the counter electrodes. A drive circuit includes a switch unit coupled to the counter electrodes through thin-film transistors. The switch unit selectively supplies a direct-current drive signal to the counter electrodes during the write period and an alternating-current drive signal to the counter electrodes during the touch sensing period. By time-divisionally controlling display driving and touch detection and by selectively switching drive signals supplied through the TFTs, the display device enables integrated display and touch sensing operation while reducing circuit complexity and improving sensing reliability.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in patent language, a display device where common electrodes also function as touch electrodes, the second scan circuit has a shift register and switch unit, and a second control signal stabilizes the gate node of a TFT during screen writing.
counterfactuals.output:
A display device may comprise a display panel including a plurality of pixels arranged in a matrix, a plurality of data lines, a plurality of gate lines, and a plurality of common electrodes. The common electrodes may be configured to receive a common voltage during a display period and to function as touch sensing electrodes during a touch sensing period.

The display device may further comprise a first scan circuit configured to sequentially supply first scan signals to a first group of gate lines, and a second scan circuit configured to supply second scan signals to a second group of gate lines. The second scan circuit may include a shift register and a switch unit. The shift register may include a plurality of stages, each stage being configured to generate an output signal in response to at least one clock signal and a start signal. The switch unit may be coupled between an output terminal of the shift register and at least one corresponding gate line, and may selectively transfer the output signal of the shift register to the corresponding gate line as a second scan signal.

Each stage of the shift register may include a thin film transistor having a gate node configured to control an output operation of the stage. During a screen writing period in which image data is written to the pixels, a second control signal may be applied to the switch unit or to a control terminal associated with the stage so as to stabilize the gate node of the thin film transistor. In particular, the second control signal may maintain the gate node at a predetermined voltage level, suppress leakage-induced voltage variation, or prevent an unintended turn-on operation of the thin film transistor while the display panel is being driven for image writing.

Accordingly, because the common electrodes are shared for display driving and touch sensing, the number of separate touch electrodes may be reduced. In addition, because the second control signal stabilizes the gate node of the thin film transistor included in the second scan circuit during the screen writing period, deterioration of scan signal reliability, abnormal gate line activation, and display defects caused by gate-node floating may be reduced or prevented.
